content: Undescended testes, a condition commonly observed in male infants, is defined as the failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotal position. This condition is more prevalent in preterm male infants, with reported rates ranging from 9% to 30%, compared to 4% to 5% in full-term male infants. The testes may be located anywhere along their normal path of descent, from the lower pole of the kidney to the superficial inguinal pouch. Based on their location, undescended testes are categorized as either palpable or impalpable. Palpable testes are typically found in the superficial inguinal pouch or the inguinal canal, while impalpable testes may reside within the inguinal canal or in the abdomen, proximal to the deep inguinal ring. Approximately 20% of undescended testes are located at or proximal to the deep inguinal ring. If left untreated, undescended testes are at risk of complications, including histological changes that can lead to subfertility, an increased risk of testicular malignancy, trauma, and torsion. Early recognition and treatment are critical to preserving long-term testicular function, as progressive damage to germ cells has been shown to occur beyond the age of two years. The primary goal of treatment is to relocate the affected testis to its anatomically correct position in the scrotum to prevent these complications. The standard treatment for undescended testes is surgical intervention, specifically orchiopexy. This procedure involves separating the processus vaginalis from the cord structures, ensuring adequate cord length, and anchoring the testis in a subdartos pouch within the scrotum. Orchiopexy has a reported success rate of approximately 90% for all undescended testes, except for those located high in the abdomen. The Fowler-Stephens technique, which involves dividing the testicular vessels to allow descent of testes with short vessels, has a success rate of about 70%. However, this technique carries a risk of ischemic loss of the testis and is now often performed as a two-stage procedure to improve testicular survival. Laparoscopy, introduced in the 1970s, has significantly advanced the management of impalpable and high intra-abdominal testes. It is now commonly used to locate impalpable testes and has contributed to the resurgence of the Fowler-Stephens orchiopexy, which can be performed as either a single-stage or two-stage procedure. Hormonal therapy is another approach used to stimulate testicular descent. Agents such as human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG), human menopausal gonadotropin, and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues have been employed, with reported success rates as high as 60% when HCG is combined with luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LH-RH). However, success rates vary, with some studies reporting rates between 25% and 35%. Hormonal therapy is typically initiated during the neonatal period but has also been shown to induce descent at later ages. While hormonal therapy may have beneficial effects on the contralateral testis, it is associated with a high incidence of side effects. The optimal timing of intervention for undescended testes remains a topic of debate. Some experts advocate for early surgical correction between three and six months of age to prevent histological changes that could impair fertility or increase the risk of malignancy. Others suggest that correction up to two years of age is sufficient to prevent long-term complications. Historically, surgical interventions were delayed beyond six months due to concerns about higher complication rates in early infancy. Current guidelines recommend surgery before the age of two years to minimize the impact on germ cell maturation. Germ cell development is an active process that continues until approximately four years of age. Testes that remain undescended are prone to progressive histological damage, including a reduction in germ cells and Leydig cells. Early relocation of the testis to the scrotum can halt this damage. However, early intervention does not appear to affect the risk of malignancy or the success of sperm extraction later in life. Hormonal therapy has also been used as an adjunct to surgical correction, with the aim of enhancing germ cell maturation in both the operated and contralateral testes. Despite its potential benefits, the precise role of hormonal therapy in the management of undescended testes remains unclear. Robust comparisons between hormonal therapy and surgical correction, as well as between different surgical techniques and recommended ages for intervention, are needed to guide clinical practice and inform future research.
